body.en: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers; a series is the sum of a sequence's terms. Arithmetic and geometric types appear in financial models, while infinite series connect to calculus through limits.

Common ratio \(r\); \(n\)-th term, finite sum, and infinite sum:

\[a_n=a_1\,r^{n-1},\quad S_n=\frac{a_1(1-r^n)}{1-r}\;(r\neq1),\quad S_\infty=\frac{a_1}{1-r}\;(|r|<1).\]

label.en: ● Precise (ε, N) Definition of Limit of a Sequence

body.en:
A sequence \(\{a_n\}\) converges to a real limit \(L\), written \(\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = L\), if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an integer \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that:

\[ n > N \implies |a_n - L| < \varepsilon. \]

Geometric Meaning: No matter how narrow an error corridor \((L - \varepsilon, L + \varepsilon)\) is chosen around \(L\), there is a cutoff index \(N\) beyond which all subsequent terms \(a_{N+1}, a_{N+2}, \dots\) are trapped permanently inside the corridor.

Example 1: Prove using the \(\varepsilon\text{--}N\) definition that \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n} = 0\).

Proof: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be given. By the Archimedean Property of the real numbers, choose an integer \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(N \ge \lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil > 0\). For any integer \(n > N\): \[ \left|\frac{1}{n} - 0\right| = \frac{1}{n} < \frac{1}{N} \le \varepsilon. \] Thus \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n} = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

Example 2: Prove that \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3n - 1}{2n + 5} = \frac{3}{2}\).

1. Scratchwork: We examine the error: \[ \left|\frac{3n - 1}{2n + 5} - \frac{3}{2}\right| = \left|\frac{2(3n - 1) - 3(2n + 5)}{2(2n + 5)}\right| = \left|\frac{6n - 2 - 6n - 15}{4n + 10}\right| = \frac{17}{4n + 10} < \frac{17}{4n}. \] We want \(\frac{17}{4n} < \varepsilon \iff 4n > \frac{17}{\varepsilon} \iff n > \frac{17}{4\varepsilon}\). Choose \(N = \lceil \frac{17}{4\varepsilon} \rceil\).

2. Formal Proof: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be arbitrary. Select \(N = \max\left(1, \left\lceil \frac{17}{4\varepsilon} \right\rceil\right)\). For any \(n > N\): \[ \left|\frac{3n - 1}{2n + 5} - \frac{3}{2}\right| = \frac{17}{4n + 10} < \frac{17}{4n} < \frac{17}{4N} \le \varepsilon. \] Hence \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3n - 1}{2n + 5} = \frac{3}{2}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Pascal's triangle rows give binomial coefficients for small \(n.\)

Finding a specific term: the \((r+1)\)-th term of \((a+b)^n\) is \(\dbinom{n}{r}a^{n-r}b^r.\)
To prove a statement \(P(n)\) for all \(n\ge1\): (1) Base case: verify \(P(1)\). (2) Inductive step: assume \(P(k)\) true, prove \(P(k+1)\) follows.

problem.en: Find the sum of the arithmetic series \(5+9+13+\cdots+101.\)
Find the term containing \(x^3\) in the expansion of \(\left(2x-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^7.\)

solution.en:
Base case \(n=1\): LHS\(=1\), RHS\(=\dfrac{1\cdot2}{2}=1.\;\checkmark\)

Inductive step: Assume true for \(n=k\): \(1+\cdots+k=\dfrac{k(k+1)}{2}.\)

For \(n=k+1\): \(1+\cdots+k+(k+1)=\dfrac{k(k+1)}{2}+(k+1)=(k+1)\!\left(\dfrac{k}{2}+1\right)=\dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}.\;\checkmark\)

label.en: ▲ Pre-Calculus Traps & Commandments — Sequences, Series & Binomial Theorem

body.en:
• Lower Index Pitfalls in Geometric Series: In \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a r^{n-1}\), the first term is \(a r^0 = a\). But in \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a r^n\), the first term is \(a_1 = ar\)! Always evaluate the true first term by substituting the initial index value rather than blindly copying the leading coefficient.
  • Infinite Series Convergence Condition: The formula \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r}\) is valid strictly when \(|r| < 1\). If \(|r| \ge 1\), the terms do not approach 0 and the series diverges. Plugging \(r = 2\) into the formula produces an invalid result.
  • Binomial Expansion Negative Signs: When expanding \((A - B)^n\), the negative sign belongs to the second term: \(\binom{n}{k} A^{n-k} (-B)^k = (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} A^{n-k} B^k\). Terms alternate signs, with odd powers of \(k\) being negative.
  • Strict Induction Logic: A proof by mathematical induction requires two distinct parts: (1) verifying the base case (usually \(n = 1\)), and (2) explicitly using the inductive hypothesis \(P(k)\) to prove \(P(k+1)\). You must show where the assumed formula for the first \(k\) terms is substituted.

question.en: Find the 6th term in the expansion of \((3x - 2y^2)^8\) in fully simplified form.

solution.en:
In the binomial theorem expansion \(\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} A^{n-k} B^k\), the 1st term has \(k = 0\), so the 6th term has \(k = 5\).

Identify terms: \(n = 8\), \(A = 3x\), \(B = -2y^2\):

\[T_6 = \binom{8}{5} (3x)^{8-5} (-2y^2)^5 = \binom{8}{3} (3x)^3 (-2y^2)^5.\]

Compute each factor:

  • \(\binom{8}{3} = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 56\)
  • \((3x)^3 = 27x^3\)
  • \((-2y^2)^5 = -32y^{10}\)

Multiply the coefficients:

\[T_6 = 56 \times 27 \times (-32) x^3 y^{10} = 56 \times (-864) x^3 y^{10} = -48384 x^3 y^{10}.\]
